prompt: In this course's lab, what answers the AWS command line?
hint: A program on your own computer.

choices.text: A free-tier AWS account the course lends you
choices.why: There is no account at all, lent or otherwise: no lesson depends on one company's free allowance.

choices.text: moto, on port 4567
choices.why: Right. An open-source imitation of the AWS API, on your own machine, holding everything in memory.

choices.text: A shell in the browser that the platform runs for every student
choices.why: The platform runs nothing for you; every command is typed on your own computer.

choices.text: AWS CloudShell, inside the AWS console
choices.why: CloudShell needs an AWS account, which is exactly what this course does without.

prompt: Which of these does moto 5.2.3 actually enforce, rather than only store? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table in the first section has two rows marked as checked.

choices.text: An explicit Deny in an identity policy, once checking is switched on
choices.why: Right. moto judges identity policies when it is started with checking on.

choices.text: The four switches of S3 Block Public Access
choices.why: moto stores them and enforces none of them, which is why the lab can show a bucket going public.

choices.text: A bucket policy that makes an object public to anonymous requests
choices.why: Right. The anonymous curl was refused, then served, then refused again.

choices.text: A condition demanding MFA
choices.why: Conditions are stored and ignored.

choices.text: A service control policy of an organisation
choices.why: Stored, never enforced.

prompt: moto lets a request through that AWS's documentation says AWS would refuse. What does a lesson in this course do with that?
hint: Silence from the imitation is not an answer from the real thing.

choices.text: It treats moto's answer as AWS's, since the API is identical
choices.why: The API is the same shape; what is enforced behind it is not. That is the gap the course marks every time.

choices.text: It leaves the topic out, because it cannot be shown
choices.why: The topic stays; it is taught from AWS's documentation and said to be so.

choices.text: It says, beside the transcript, what AWS would do instead, citing AWS's documentation and marking it as not run
choices.why: Right. The run shows what moto does; the prose says where AWS differs and that the claim was not run.

choices.text: It writes the output AWS would have printed into the transcript
choices.why: Never. A transcript is what a machine printed; invented output is the one thing a course cannot do.

prompt: Which path to a terminal on Ubuntu 24.04 does the course recommend, unless you are on a Mac?
hint: The cheapest one for your computer that still matches the transcripts.

choices.text: A virtual machine in a hypervisor
choices.why: That is the Mac's path, and the one for a computer you would rather not touch. It costs 2 GB of memory while it runs.

choices.text: Installed: Ubuntu itself, or Ubuntu under WSL
choices.why: Right. It costs some disk and moto's memory, and nothing else.

choices.text: A rented shell online, since nothing touches your computer
choices.why: It works, but it depends on somebody's account and terms, and the course recommends nothing that does.

prompt: Why does the lab want two terminals instead of one?
hint: One of them is busy for as long as something runs.

choices.text: moto occupies one and prints a line for every request; the other is where you type
choices.why: Right, and that first terminal is the closest thing the lab has to an audit log.

choices.text: The AWS command line refuses to run in the same terminal that started moto, so a second one is required
choices.why: Nothing refuses; moto simply holds that terminal while it runs.

choices.text: Each terminal holds a different AWS account
choices.why: Both talk to the same moto, with the same account.

choices.text: To keep the two `test` keys apart
choices.why: Both terminals read the same env.sh and carry the same placeholder key.

prompt: Why does `env.sh` set the credentials to `test` and `test` instead of leaving them empty?
hint: Think about the request that escapes to AWS by mistake.

choices.text: moto refuses to start unless both are exactly `test`
choices.why: moto accepts any key at all until lesson 6 switches its checking on.

choices.text: Because AWS accepts them for free accounts
choices.why: AWS refuses them: there is no such key.

choices.text: So a request that reaches AWS by mistake fails instead of acting on an account
choices.why: Right. The failure section shows it: InvalidClientTokenId, and nothing created or charged.

choices.text: The command line needs some value to sign with, and any word would do
choices.why: It does need a value, but the point of these is that AWS refuses them; a real key would not fail.

prompt: Match each line of `env.sh` to what it does.
hint: The table under the file.

pairs.right: sends every request to moto instead of AWS
picks São Paulo for every command
prints long answers straight to the terminal
gives moto the policies AWS maintains

prompt: Against moto, `aws sts get-caller-identity` named the user `moto` in account `123456789012`. Why that user?
hint: Nothing has been created yet.

choices.text: Because env.sh named it
choices.why: env.sh sets a key, not a user name.

choices.text: moto accepts any key and attributes it to its default user
choices.why: Right. Until checking is on, every key is moto's own user.

choices.text: It is the account's root user, which every new account starts with
choices.why: A root user's ARN ends in `:root`, not `user/moto`.

choices.text: The `test` key was created for a user called moto during installation
choices.why: Nothing was created during installation; moto is empty when it starts.

prompt: A student unsets `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` and runs `aws sts get-caller-identity`. They get `InvalidClientTokenId`. Where did the request go?
hint: The command line's default destination.

choices.text: Nowhere: the command line refused to send it
choices.why: It was sent; the error is the answer that came back.

choices.text: To moto, which rejected the key
choices.why: moto accepts any key until checking is on; and without the variable the request does not go to moto.

choices.text: To AWS's real security token service
choices.why: Right. AWS refused the placeholder key, and nothing was created or charged.

prompt: Match each message to what it means.
hint: Four of the failures were produced on purpose.

pairs.right: this terminal has not read env.sh

pairs.left: `Could not connect to the endpoint URL`

right_distractors: the AWS CLI is the wrong version

prompt: `apt-get` says it could not get a lock a minute after the machine started. What is the right move?
hint: Something else is installing packages.

choices.text: Delete the lock file and run the command again
choices.why: That is the advice found online, and how a package database gets damaged.

choices.text: Wait a few minutes and run it again
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu is installing its own updates, and only one program may install at a time.

choices.text: Reinstall Ubuntu, because the archive is broken
choices.why: Nothing is broken; another installer holds the lock.

choices.text: Run it with `--force` so it ignores the other installer
choices.why: There is no safe way to install alongside another installer; waiting is the fix.

prompt: Why is identity called the new perimeter in the cloud?
hint: Where are the controls, and what decides who may use them?

choices.text: The provider's buildings are guarded by identity cards
choices.why: The building stopped mattering; the controls are not in it.

choices.text: Because the management API is reachable from the internet, and the credential decides
choices.why: Right. Who can reach the controls became who holds a valid key.

choices.text: Every cloud resource is named after the user who created it
choices.why: Nothing of the kind; names are free text.

choices.text: Firewalls cannot be configured in the cloud, so who may sign in is the only control left
choices.why: They can; they are settings like everything else. They just no longer stand between a key and the API.

prompt: Which of these are differences the lesson names between a data centre and a cloud? Choose all that apply.
hint: Six things move; the ideas do not.

choices.text: A resource can live for minutes, and its address goes to somebody else after
choices.why: Right. So what you will want to know afterwards has to be recorded while it happens.

choices.text: Least privilege no longer applies
choices.why: It applies everywhere; only where it is enforced changes, to a policy on an identity.

choices.text: You cannot mirror a switch port or tap a cable
choices.why: Right. What you see is what the provider offers to record.

choices.text: A bill ten times last month's can be a security signal
choices.why: Right. A stolen key is often put to mining cryptocurrency.

choices.text: Confidentiality, integrity and availability stop being useful words
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: none of the ideas is retired.

prompt: A company moves a file share from its own data centre to cloud storage, and keeps the same firewall team and the same change board. What protection did it lose in the move, according to the lesson?
hint: Count who has to agree before the files reach the internet.

choices.text: Encryption of the files, which cloud storage does not offer
choices.why: Cloud storage offers it; lesson 11 is about it. That is not what moved.

choices.text: The people who stood in front of the decision: one request now publishes the files
choices.why: Right. The firewall team and the board are still there, and the bucket policy does not pass through either.

choices.text: Nothing, since the same teams still approve every change
choices.why: They approve the changes that reach them. A bucket policy is a call to an API, and it reaches nobody.

choices.text: Physical security, which is now somebody else's
choices.why: Physical security moved to the provider and is done well. It was never what stood between the files and the internet.

prompt: In the lab, moto answered with a default VPC in how many regions?
hint: The loop counted them.

prompt: The anonymous `curl` returned `403`, then `200` after one call. What was that call?
hint: It allowed one action to a principal written as a star.

choices.text: `create-bucket` with a public flag
choices.why: The bucket already existed and was private; the 403 proved it.

choices.text: `put-bucket-policy` allowing `s3:GetObject` to `"Principal": "*"`
choices.why: Right. A star as the principal means everybody, signed in or not.

choices.text: `aws s3 cp` of the file a second time
choices.why: Uploading again changes nothing about who may read it.

choices.text: Turning off Block Public Access, which had protected the bucket since it was created
choices.why: moto enforces none of Block Public Access, so there was nothing to turn off; the policy alone did it.

prompt: Against a new real AWS bucket, what would have happened to that same `put-bucket-policy`?
hint: A guardrail AWS now switches on by default, and moto does not enforce.

choices.text: Accepted, exactly as moto did
choices.why: moto accepted it because it enforces none of Block Public Access.

choices.text: Refused, by Block Public Access
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9 is the decade of incidents that made it the default.

choices.text: Accepted, with a warning printed on the terminal
choices.why: The lesson's point is that the command printed nothing; and on AWS it would not have been accepted.

choices.text: Held for approval by the account's root user
choices.why: There is no approval step in the API; a request is allowed or refused.

prompt: caio says he removed the public policy from a bucket an hour ago. Which piece of evidence does the lesson ask for before you call it fixed?
hint: Prove a fix the way the fault was found.

choices.text: A screenshot of the bucket's settings page in the console, with no policy shown
choices.why: That shows one setting. An object can still be public by another route, and only asking finds out.

choices.text: caio's word, given in the team's channel
choices.why: A claim, not evidence.

choices.text: An anonymous request for an object, answered with `403`
choices.why: Right. Ask again as the stranger and read the answer.

choices.text: The output of `aws s3api delete-bucket-policy`, which prints success
choices.why: It prints nothing at all, as the transcript shows; and a command succeeding says nothing about what a stranger can read.

prompt: In a bucket policy, `"Principal": "___"` means everybody, signed in or not.
hint: One character.

prompt: Put the steps of the section's experiment in the order they ran.
hint: The fix is proved the way the fault was found.
items: upload the export to a private bucket
ask for it anonymously and get 403
attach a policy allowing everybody to read
ask anonymously again and get the file
ask anonymously once more and get 403
trap: Stopping at "delete the policy" is the slip: the last anonymous request is the proof.
